metric_rationale: The design contains three families of trials on which a lexicographic one-reason rule and a unit-weight counting rule make opposite (or differently determinate) commitments: (i) pairs 1-4, where the single top cue is pitted against a coalition of 1-4 lower cues; (ii) pairs 9-12, where the first discriminating cue sits lower in the cascade and all remaining cues favour the other option; and (iii) pairs 5-6, where the tally is exactly even so a counting rule must guess at 50/50 whatever its parameters, while the cue cascade is fully decisive. The metric pools exactly these trials (agreement controls 7-8 are excluded, since both rules pick the same option there and they only dilute the contrast) and reports the proportion of choices going to the option favoured by the first discriminating cue. Under Take The Best this is (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2 on every included trial, i.e. high (~0.85 averaged over the parameter ranges) and tight, because each subject contributes 80 trials. Under Tallying it is the complement of the tally-consistent probability on the directional-conflict trials (~0.09) and exactly 0.5 on the two tie pairs, giving ~0.17 overall. Both theories' per-subject spread is driven mainly by the lapse rate, which shifts the two values toward 0.5 by comparable, modest amounts, so the ~0.68 mean gap dwarfs the between-subject variance. Mirror-image pairs are included in equal numbers, so any A/B key bias cancels and cannot inflate or deflate the score for either theory.

Two diagnostic trial families are contrasted within subject, which cancels overall lapse/noise level and sharpens the model split.

(1) Tally-tie trials (pairs 7/8 and 9/10): each option wins exactly the same number of cues, so Tallying is forced to exactly 50/50 for ANY beta and epsilon, while TTB is decisive (cue .93 beats cue .60; cue .87 beats cues .78/.70). I score the proportion of choices for the TTB-designated winner here: 0.5 under Tallying (only binomial jitter over 24 trials), ~0.85 under TTB.

(2) Large-margin disagreement trials (pairs 3/4, 5/6, 11/12): the tally favours the coalition option by 2-4 cues while TTB's top discriminating cue favours the other option. I score the proportion of choices for the tally winner: high (~0.85-0.95) under Tallying because the softmax is driven by beta*margin, near 0.15 under TTB.

The metric is the difference (2) - (1). Tallying predicts a clearly positive value (~+0.35); TTB predicts a strongly negative value (~-0.70), and because under TTB both terms are driven by the same beta and epsilon they move in opposite directions, amplifying rather than blurring the gap. The tie term is parameter-free for Tallying, so my side's variance is dominated by binomial noise alone, keeping the per-subject estimate tight at N=25.

The metric is a parameter-free behavioural index restricted to trials where the two options win on EXACTLY the same number of cues (unit-tally ties) but where the validity-weighted margin is clearly non-zero (|d| >= 0.15 with squared validities; this selects the base pairs {H1,H2} vs {L2,L3}, {H1,L1} vs {M,L3}, {H2,L1} vs {M,L2} and their A/B mirrors, and discards the near-zero-margin pair {H1,L3} vs {H2,L1}). On these trials I score the proportion of choices for the option holding the higher-validity cue set.

Tallying's softmax over equal tallies is EXACTLY uniform for every value of beta and epsilon, so it predicts 0.50 with no parameter-driven between-subject spread at all (only binomial noise over ~36 such trials, var ~0.007). AVAI, in contrast, integrates the continuous weighted difference, so it should land at ~0.89-0.98 across the plausible gamma/beta ranges, again with small between-subject spread. The mean gap is ~0.43 with per-subject SDs under 0.09, giving a decisive Welch test at N=25. It is not trivially true of AVAI: any model that binarises cue-wise winners (Tallying, Equal-Weight on signs, coin-flip-on-ties) must yield 0.5, whereas any validity-weighted or lexicographic integrator yields values well above 0.5; the metric measures a real behavioural phenomenon (magnitude sensitivity on count-tied trials) rather than model fit.

The design contains tally-TIE trials (each option wins exactly the same number of expert comparisons) that nevertheless carry a LARGE validity-weighted margin: base 7 / its mirror, where one option wins only on the .97 expert and the other only on the .53 expert. Tallying's softmax is exactly uniform whenever the two counts are equal, for ANY beta and epsilon, so the predicted proportion of choices for the option holding the high-validity cue is exactly 0.50 \u2014 a parameter-free prediction. AVAI acts on the continuous weighted difference (d \u2248 +0.66 with gamma=2), giving p \u2248 0.95\u20130.99 for that same option across its whole parameter range. I deliberately exclude the other tie structure (H1+L3 vs H2+L1, |d| \u2248 0.02) via the 0.30 threshold, because both theories predict chance there and it would only dilute the contrast. Each subject contributes 12 such trials, so per-subject binomial noise is small (var of the proportion \u2264 0.021 for Tallying, ~0.003 for AVAI), while the mean gap is ~0.47 \u2014 large mean separation with tight per-subject spread. The metric is well defined on a single subject's slice and on the pooled frame.

This is the dominance-accuracy metric: the proportion of trials on which the subject picks the option favoured by EVERY discriminating expert row (trials 13-18 here: |D| = 2, 4, and 6, all cues agreeing). Under AVAI the weighted evidence difference on such trials is large and grows with the number of agreeing cues, so choice is at ceiling (p ~ 0.98-1.00 for any admissible gamma/beta, limited only by the small epsilon lapse). Under RDS the choice on a dominance trial is correct only when the subject does not lose the thread: the conflict-interference term forces guessing at rate 1-(1-eps0)*rho^(m-2), giving ~0.86 at |D|=2, ~0.72 at |D|=4 and ~0.63 at |D|=6, i.e. a pooled value near 0.74. The metric therefore has a ~0.25 mean gap. It is also tight per subject: 30 trials contribute per subject, and both theories' parameter ranges move the expected value by only a few points, so per-subject variance is essentially binomial (~0.007 for RDS, ~0.0003 for AVAI), which comfortably clears Welch's test at N=25. It is not trivially true for AVAI because unanimous-cue accuracy is a plain behavioural quantity that any one-reason or non-interfering model could equally produce at ceiling; only RDS's specific claim that difficulty grows with the COUNT of differing rows (rather than their diagnosticity) predicts a substantial sub-ceiling value here.

Isolates the 'crown jewel' trial family (design bases 3 and 4 and their mirrors: trials 5-8) via a purely structural filter: exactly two discriminating columns, pointing to opposite options, with the LATER column carrying the LOWER validity (0.95 early vs 0.55 late). On these displays the two theories make opposite, near-deterministic predictions.

AVAI integrates weighted validity, so it must pick the option holding the 0.95 cue regardless of column position: weighted difference |d| = 0.95^gamma - 0.55^gamma ~ 0.60, beta*|d| ~ 3-5, so p(later-cue option) ~ 0.02-0.05, essentially independent of where the rows sit. RDS instead lets recency x distinctiveness decide: the later, lower-validity row has salience ratio exp(lambda*5)*(0.45)^delta vs exp(0)*(0.05)^delta, i.e. thousands to one, so the later-cue option is picked with probability ~ (1-eps0) + eps0/2 ~ 0.85 (m=2 means minimal conflict interference).

Predicted values: ~0.85 under RDS vs ~0.03 under AVAI, a gap of ~0.8. Because 24 trials per subject enter the average and both theories are near-deterministic on them, per-subject variance is tiny (binomial ~0.005 for RDS, ~0.001 for AVAI, plus negligible parameter spread), so the contrast is both large in mean and tight across subjects. Crucially it is not trivially true for RDS: any position-blind integrator (including tallying, Bayesian weighting, or plain TTB) would land far below 0.5 here, so a value near 0.85 in humans is diagnostic of position-driven, redundancy-discounted one-reason choice.

The design duplicates every stated validity, so OCO-LI's individuation gate is exactly phi=0: the odd-cue-out/recency anchoring competition cannot run and choices collapse to a probability-matched tally over the discriminating rows. RDS has no such gate, so its salience weights exp(lam*j)*(1-v)^delta (spanning ~5 orders of magnitude here) make the LAST-READ discriminating row essentially decide the trial.

The metric is the rate of choosing the option favoured by the highest-index (last-read) discriminating row, computed only on conflict displays (at least one row favouring each option) and excluding the unanimous baseline trials 1-4, where both theories make identical predictions and which would only dilute the contrast.

Predicted values (using mid-range parameters): OCO-LI gives exactly 0.50 on the eight m=2 split-tie pairs (parameter-free, since the flat tally is 1/1 and the guess mixture preserves 0.5), ~0.41 on the m=3 pairs (tally 2:1 against the late row) and ~0.39 on the m=4 pairs (tally 3:1 against the late row), for an overall value near 0.46-0.47. RDS gives ~0.70-0.86 on the m=2 pairs, ~0.78 on m=3 and ~0.72 on m=4, overall near 0.79. That is a ~0.32 gap.

Precision is high because the metric pools 72 trials per subject (12 unique pairs x 6 reps), so per-subject binomial noise is ~0.06 SD, and OCO-LI's dominant component (the m=2 ties at exactly 0.5) is completely parameter-independent, keeping between-subject variance tiny. Direction of the metric is not trivially tied to either model's mechanism label: it is a purely descriptive 'last-differing-row' choice rate that any theory can be scored on.

The two theories share everything except OCO-LI's label-individuation gate, which in this near-duplicate-validity design forces phi ~ 0.16, i.e. ~85% probability matching to the raw proportion of discriminating rows. So the decisive question is: on trials where the row-count tally and the single most salient (late, low-validity) discriminating row point in different directions (or the tally is exactly tied and thus uninformative), do choices follow the salient row or hug the tally?

The metric selects exactly those conflict trials (tally tied, or tally majority opposite to the highest-salience discriminating row, using the design's known validities with lam=1.6, delta=0.9) and reports the proportion of choices that follow the salient-row owner. This selection automatically drops the two unanimous baseline bases (where both models agree) and keeps bases 3-9, ~70 of 90 trials per subject, so the metric is tight per subject (binomial with ~70 observations).

Quantitative predictions from the two generative models with central parameters: RDS ~ 0.73-0.76 (salience essentially owns the decision; only the conflict-interference lapse pulls it down), OCO-LI ~ 0.50 (its 84% ungated component is pinned to the tally, which by construction opposes or is neutral w.r.t. the salient row). A ~0.24 gap with per-subject SD around 0.05-0.07 gives a very large Welch t at N=25. The metric is also mirror-symmetric (each base appears with its A/B mirror), so side bias cannot inflate or deflate it.
